title: GOP leaders fume after members who lost reelection are no-shows | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

In one of Republicans’ final weeks in power, GOP leaders couldn’t convince enough of their members to come back to Washington to actually vote on their own bills — and Rep. Greg Murphy was furious.

Murphy, who just lost his eastern North Carolina seat in one of the biggest upsets of the midterms, unleashed on his GOP colleagues in a closed-door meeting Wednesday, urging leadership to cut off pay for any lawmakers who don’t show up, according to multiple people in the room.

“Look, I lost. I’m still here. I’m still here,” Murphy later told CNN about his frustrations at some of his colleagues’ delinquency. “If they aren’t here, they shouldn’t get paid.”

After their historic midterm rout, Republicans are increasingly exasperated at their otherwise-healthy GOP colleagues who are refusing to come back to Washington after their election defeats.

Speaker Mike Johnson and his GOP leadership team have been privately reprimanding those who chose not to come back, including one member — Florida Rep. Anna Paulina Luna – who told the speaker she did not return because she was worried about aCNN reportof the prospect of an Iranian “dirty bomb” plot in Washington, according to three sources familiar with the matter.

Johnson, who has had aparticularly contentious relationshipwith Luna, when learning of the reason for her absence reminded the congresswoman that her staff was in Washington working, according to a person familiar with the discussions. CNN has reached out to Luna’s office for comment.

“Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” Johnson said Thursday. “We had 14 absences yesterday, so it’s not possible for us to advance a rule and advance our legislative agenda unless the members are here doing their job. … We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can’t do that unless people are present at work.”

It’s a glaring —and familiar— problem for Hill GOP leaders, who struggled all year trying to keep a record-small majority in line. And it comes as Republicans were already struggling with how to achieve as much of President Donald Trump’s agenda as possible before being pushed deep into the minority in January.

Republican leaders are under pressure to replenish Pentagon funding after months of war with Iran, but they don’t have the votes. They want to use their GOP trifecta to raise the debt limit to avoid a Democratic showdown with Trump next year. And they want to accomplish big legacy items, like permitting reform, before they’re forced to start over with Democrats in charge.

House Republicans believe the best way to accomplish Trump’s wants — particularly on the debt limit and Pentagon funding for the war — is by sidestepping Democrats altogether and doing a party-line bill. But any party-line bill is logistically challenging in the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune has put a pause on his party’s push to take that route.

Now, Hill Republicans are increasingly worried they could squander their final days in power, with absences further complicating an already-difficult December puzzle. Some in GOP leadership privately fear that the only things Republicans will accomplish in December is punting government funding into the new year – maybe paired with an extension of the nation’s expired spy powers, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions.

They also worry about political theatre that could distract from the agenda, with GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a frequent leadership antagonist, forcing votes on the Epstein files and ending the Iran war.

Already, there’s some talk of sending the House home after passing a stopgap bill ahead of the December 11 funding deadline – and canceling the following weeks’ worth of scheduled votes – because Republicans won’t have the votes to do more, according to several of those people.

“There’s a possibility we can squander it if we don’t get our members back here,” senior GOP Rep. Mike Simpson said about the remaining days of Republican control. “What do we do to these guys that won’t come back?”

Rep. Jim Jordan, the incoming House GOP minority leader, is among the Republicans pushing to use that party-line process — known as reconciliation — to get Trump priorities done before the Democratic takeover.

“I’m in favor of getting as much done as we possibly can,” Jordan told CNN when asked about his preference for a GOP-only bill, adding he wants to see “all kinds of important things, like debt ceiling issue, like the defense issue.”

Asked whether that would include funding for Iran, Jordan added: “That’s certainly important.”

Thune, for his part, said Thursday that they likely won’t move ahead on a party-line bill until after Thanksgiving — when both chambers will have just three work weeks left. Many Republicans see it as a tacit acknowledgement that the party won’t get anything substantive done before handing over the gavels.

In the Senate, Republicans are squarely focused on confirming more Trump judges, landing a long-awaited permitting reform bill and finding a way to get money for the Pentagon.

Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota said he and others are still hoping Democrats will be willing to help pass some of that Pentagon funding — even as an emboldened Senate Democratic caucus makes clear that it won’t approve more money for the Iran war.

“They can vote against the military and tell everybody why they’re doing it,” Hoeven said of Democrats. “We’re trying to give them an opportunity to join us and do the right thing, which is vote support our military.”

If that doesn’t work, Hoeven acknowledged Republicans will need to try again on the party-line reconciliation push despite its difficulty.

But GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas was blunt about the prospects for that bill: “Everybody recognizes this is going to be a Herculean effort trying to get the House and the Senate to agree on the scope and the process.”

And Murphy, the North Carolina Republican chiding his colleagues for their absences, added this: “It’ll be hard if people don’t show up to their job.”

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer, Ted Barrett, Aileen Graef, Manu Raju and Logan Schiciano contributed to this report.

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer, Ted Barrett, Aileen Graef, Manu Raju and Logan Schiciano contributed to this report.
